summary:
Nasarawa State stands under Nigeria's national framework. The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 (SSMPA) applies across the country and reaches well beyond marriage: Human Rights Watch (October 2016) records that it also bans cohabitation between same-sex partners, any public show of a same-sex amorous relationship, and the operation of gay organisations, with penalties of 10 to 14 years' imprisonment, and that police have used it to justify torture and arbitrary arrests.

Criminal exposure attaches at entry. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on Nigeria (June 2025, updated April 2026) records that same-sex sex between men is criminalised under secular law with up to 14 years' imprisonment, and that Sharia law in all twelve northern states criminalises same-sex acts between men and between women, with male sodomy carrying the death penalty under state Zina provisions.

The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office's travel advisory for Nigeria (19 August 2026, carried by Sahara Reporters) warns LGBT+ travellers of arrest, violence, attacks, blackmail and intimidation. Same-sex sexual activity is illegal and can attract up to 14 years' imprisonment, and the federal law extends to people who arrange, attend or conduct same-sex weddings and to those involved with gay groups or organisations. Some northern states operate Sharia law under which same-sex activity can attract the death penalty, and breaching curfews or movement restrictions risks arrest and detention.

Trans identity is not explicitly criminalised in the national statute, but gender expression is exposed. Reuters (September 2022) reports that transgender Nigerians live in fear of proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public; whether those proposals have been enacted is not settled by the sources available here.

Violence against trans people is documented and enforcement outcomes are weak. On 9 August 2024 the beaten body of a 33-year-old transgender TikToker known as Abuja Area Mama was found along the Katampe–Mabushi expressway in the capital, roughly a year after she had said she feared for her life; police announced an investigation and described the deceased as a man fully dressed in female clothing, while the Abuja police chief ordered a thorough and discreet investigation. The Dial (February 2025) records that six months after the killing no suspects had been charged.

Formal constitutional guarantees of non-discrimination and of private and family life do not translate into protection in practice. Mass arrests and detention of LGBTQ+ people are common, especially in northern states, and Nigeria offers no statutory protection for LGBTQ+ people; the SSMPA reinforced colonial-era criminalisation.
tangentialFactors:
Visitors who use dating apps face entrapment independent of official enforcement. The Thomson Reuters Foundation (April 2024) documents kito gangs that lure LGBTQ+ Nigerians through Grindr and similar apps to meetings where victims are beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing.

Police violence against perceived gay people is a routine feature of how the law is applied. TimesLIVE (March 2025) reports that Okafor, a 24-year-old man stopped by police in Lagos, was struck in the mouth with a police gun butt and released only after paying almost half of the 50,000 naira bribe demanded, for looking gay. That incident occurred in another state and stands as one data point within a national pattern in which those affected describe the SSMPA as a weaponised law producing a climate of hostility independent of its text.

The UK Foreign Office advisory of August 2026 aligns with the warnings carried by Human Rights Watch and the UK Home Office, so the risk picture presented to travellers matches the picture presented to asylum claimants and rights researchers. Direction of travel is toward heightened traveller-facing warning rather than relaxation.
localsOnly:
Bobrisky (Idris Okuneye), Nigeria's most prominent transgender woman, pleaded guilty to four counts of naira abuse on 5 April 2024 and was sentenced on 12 April 2024 to the maximum six months with no option of fine. She served the sentence in a maximum-security prison in Lagos and was released on 5 August 2024.

Placement of trans detainees is left to official discretion. Press coverage at sentencing openly asked which prison the authorities would keep the crossdresser in, indicating that assignment between male and female sections was not governed by a published rule. An October 2024 investigative panel dismissed bribery allegations against her but found that housing her in a maximum-security prison violated the Nigerian Correctional Service Act because she was a first-time offender.

Residents live under constitutional guarantees of non-discrimination and of private and family life, but these are routinely overridden in practice by SSMPA-based arrest and by police demands for bribes. No domestic statute offers LGBTQ+ Nigerians a remedy against assault, extortion or arbitrary detention.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether Nasarawa State itself operates Sharia criminal law, and is therefore within the twelve northern states identified by the UK Home Office as carrying the death penalty for male sodomy, is not established by the sources assembled here. The sources speak only of the national pattern.

Whether the proposals to criminalise public cross-dressing reported by Reuters in September 2022 have since been enacted into law remains unresolved; no source in this inventory confirms enactment or withdrawal.

No Nasarawa-specific enforcement record, state police directive, or state-level prosecution of a trans or gender-nonconforming person appears in the sources assembled here. All enforcement evidence in this record originates from Abuja, Lagos or national reporting.

The outcome of the police investigation announced after the killing of Abuja Area Mama in August 2024 is not sourced beyond the February 2025 finding that no suspects had been charged.

Bobrisky's assigned cell section during her 2024 imprisonment is not stated in the sources, so her placement between male and female accommodation cannot be confirmed.
